subject: playwright
title: Test isolation
description: Browser contexts, fixtures, storageState, worker scope — and the shared state that makes a suite order-dependent.

content.title: One context per test
content.body: Every test gets a fresh BrowserContext: its own cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage and permissions, in a browser process shared with other tests. That is what makes tests independent by default, and it is also what you give up the moment you reach for module-level state.

content.title: Signing in once
content.body: Logging in through the UI in every test is the single biggest waste of time in most suites. Do it once in global setup, save the storage state, and reuse it.

content.title: Watch out
content.body: Isolation stops at the browser. Tests that write to the same database row, the same account or the same feature flag are still coupled — and with parallel workers they now race as well as depend on order.

exercises.question: Two tests run in the same file. What do they share by default?

answers.text: Nothing — each gets its own context, cookies and storage
Cookies, because the browser is the same process
localStorage, but not cookies
Everything, unless test.describe.configure is used

exercises.explanation: The browser process is reused for speed; the context is not. Anything shared between those tests came from your own code or from the backend.

exercises.question: The second test fails when run alone but passes in the full file. What is wrong?

answers.text: Line 8 — template literals are not allowed in goto
Nothing is wrong; tests always run in order
Line 1 — a module variable couples the two tests, so the second cannot run on its own or on another worker
Line 4 — createOrder should be awaited twice

exercises.explanation: Playwright may run them on different workers, in a different order, or one alone on a retry. Create what the test needs inside the test, or in a fixture.

exercises.question: What does `{ scope: 'worker' }` change about this fixture?

answers.text: It is created once per worker process and shared by every test that worker runs
It is created once for the whole run, across all workers
It is created per test, but torn down later
It disables parallelism for that fixture

exercises.explanation: Worker scope is for expensive, read-only setup — a token, a seeded tenant. Anything a test mutates belongs in test scope, or the isolation is gone again.

exercises.question: When a test is retried, it gets a brand new browser context.
exercises.explanation: A retry re-runs the test fully, fixtures included. That is also why a test that only passes on retry usually depends on state another test left behind.

exercises.question: This describe block genuinely needs its tests to run in order on one worker. Complete the configuration.

answers.text: serial
ordered
sequential
single

exercises.explanation: In serial mode a failure skips the rest of the block. It is a legitimate tool for a real multi-step wizard — and a common way to paper over accidental coupling.

exercises.question: What does storageState capture?

answers.text: Cookies and localStorage for the origins visited
Only cookies
Cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage
The whole browser profile including cache

exercises.explanation: sessionStorage is deliberately not included — it is per-tab by definition. Apps that keep their token there need it injected with an init script instead.

exercises.question: Complete the line that hands the value to the test and resumes for teardown afterwards.

answers.text: use
provide
yield
inject

exercises.explanation: Everything before use() is setup and everything after is teardown, which runs even when the test fails. That is the cleanest place to delete the data the test created.

exercises.question: What does a fixture give you that a beforeEach hook does not?

answers.text: It is typed, composable, and only runs for tests that actually request it
It runs faster
It can be asynchronous
It runs after the test instead of before

exercises.explanation: A beforeEach runs for every test in scope whether it needs the setup or not, and communicates through shared variables. Fixtures are lazy and their values arrive as typed arguments.

exercises.question: Playwright · configuration
exercises.back: Tests inside one file also run in parallel, not just across files
exercises.explanation: It turns accidental in-file coupling into a failure immediately rather than six months later. Worth enabling early, while the suite is small.

exercises.question: Why is the second version more reliable for a test about the order list?

answers.text: B — the setup no longer depends on the create form, which this test is not about
B — API calls are always faster than UI ones
A — testing through the UI is always more realistic
They are equivalent

exercises.explanation: Speed is a bonus; the point is blast radius. With A, a change to the create form fails every test that merely needed an order to exist.

exercises.question: Running with four workers is safe as long as every test creates its own data.
exercises.explanation: Not if the data collides — a fixed email, a single test account, a global feature flag. Unique per-test identifiers, or a per-worker tenant, are what make it safe.

exercises.question: Every test in the suite is suddenly signed in as the admin. Which line explains it?
exercises.code:
1  export default defineConfig({
2    use: { storageState: '.auth/admin.json' },
3    projects: [
4      { name: 'user', use: { storageState: '.auth/user.json' } },
5      { name: 'anonymous' },
6    ],
7  });

answers.text: Line 4 — a project cannot override storageState
Line 5 — the anonymous project inherits the top-level admin state
Line 2 — top-level use is ignored
Line 3 — projects must all define storageState

exercises.explanation: Project-level use merges over the top-level one, so a project that says nothing inherits it. Give the anonymous project storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] }.
